concepts.gloss: One of the three non-finite clause classifications based on its head verb form: infinitival, gerund-participial or past-participial.
An infinitival clause whose VP contains the subordinator to.
An infinitival clause with a plain-form verb and no VP subordinator to; mainly licensed in a limited set of constructions.
The prohibition on auxiliary do as an infinitival negator, contrasted with finite negative imperatives.
The perfect auxiliary have as part of a permitted non-finite infinitival, gerund-participial, or perfect participial structure.
The progressive auxiliary is compatible with infinitivals and with perfect participial structures but not productive as an internal gerund-participial auxiliary.
The passive auxiliary is permitted in infinitivals and gerund-participials, and inside perfect-participial structures.
A past-participial construction headed by perfect use of a past participle, usually complement of perfect have.
A non-finite past-participial construction headed by passive use of a past participle without its own auxiliary.
A non-finite clause whose predicate VP is its only overt nucleus constituent and that has no expressed subject.
A VP functioning as a pre-head attributive modifier inside an NP rather than as a clause.
An open or closed subordinate interrogative with a to-infinitival form.
A wh or non-wh relative construction with a to-infinitival verb.
A non-finite clause functioning as complement in clause, AdjP, NP or PP structure.
A non-finite clause modifying a clause or nominal instead of functioning as a selected complement.
A non-finite clause expressing a supplementary comment detached from a clause's integrated syntax.

rules.concept: supportive do excluded from non-finite infinitival clauses
rules.statement: A non-finite infinitival clause cannot contain supportive auxiliary do as its negative marker; infinitival negation uses not, while finite imperatives may use supportive do.
rules.condition: When an embedded to-infinitival is negated, use not with the infinitival VP rather than supportive do; contrast this with finite imperative negation, which uses don't. Lexical do meaning 'perform' is not supportive do.
rules.violation: A non-finite to-infinitival uses supportive do or don't to form its negation instead of not.

correct.text: The director asked Maya not to interrupt.
We intend not to discuss the issue today.
Don't interrupt the speaker. [finite negative imperative, not a non-finite clause]

incorrect.text: *The director asked Maya to don't interrupt.
*We intend to don't discuss the issue today.

rules.statement: Infinitival clauses allow perfect have, progressive be, and passive be, although modal auxiliaries and supportive do are excluded from non-finite clause structures.
rules.condition: When classifying auxiliary combinations inside a to-infinitival, recognise perfect have with a past-participial complement, progressive be with a gerund-participial complement, and passive be with a passive past-participial complement; distinguish these from an excluded modal auxiliary or supportive do.

contrast.text: The runners expect to have completed the course by noon. [perfect have]
The technician expects to be examining the device all morning. [progressive be]
The technician expects to be examined by the supervisor. [passive be]
The technician expects to examine the device tomorrow. [simple infinitival]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: The corresponding Burton-Roberts source material or concept index was unavailable, so no cross-framework equivalence is asserted.

rules.statement: In established Present-day English, a gerund-participial clause may contain perfect have or passive be but does not admit progressive be as its auxiliary.
rules.condition: Inside a gerund-participial clause headed by an -ing form, allow perfect having + participle and passive being + past participle; exclude being + a progressive gerund-participle as a productive auxiliary construction in established Present-day English, while recording rare casual attestations separately.
rules.violation: A gerund-participial clause contains auxiliary being followed by a gerund-participle to express the progressive construction in established Present-day English.

exceptions.description: Progressive being plus an -ing lexical verb is occasionally encountered in casual speech, but the source explicitly says that it is not an established construction in Present-day English.

correct.text: I regret having left the keys inside. [perfect have]
She disliked being watched during the rehearsal. [passive be]
I remembered waiting outside at noon. [simple gerund-participial]

incorrect.text: *I regretted being having left the keys inside. [progressive be applied to perfect have is not the established gerund-participial pattern]
*I remembered being waiting outside at noon. [progressive be inside gerund-participial]

contrast.text: She missed the bus through not being standing at the right stop. [rare casual pattern, not established in Present-day English]

rules.statement: Past-participial clauses headed by perfect participles may combine with progressive or passive be, whereas clauses headed by passive past participles do not contain auxiliaries.
rules.condition: When a past-participial clause is a complement of perfect have, identify perfect participial structure, possibly including progressive or passive be; when a past-participial clause is a passive construction such as an NP followed by checked by the editor, classify its head as a passive past participle without an auxiliary within that dependent clause.

contrast.text: The pianist has [rehearsed the piece]. [perfect past-participial]
The pianist has [been rehearsing the piece]. [perfect with progressive be]
The piece has [been rehearsed]. [perfect with passive be]
They had the report [checked by an editor]. [passive past-participial complement without its own auxiliary]

rules.concept: subjectless non-finite clauses are VP-headed clauses
rules.statement: A non-finite clause can consist solely of a VP and need not contain an overt subject, because Cambridge treats the subject as optional in non-finite clause structure.
rules.condition: When an infinitival, gerund-participial or past-participial constituent without an expressed subject functions as a complement or post-head modifier, classify the VP-headed constituent as a clause where the construction supports clausal status rather than rejecting it for lacking a subject.

contrast.text: It was a pleasure to meet the new conductor. [subjectless infinitival clause]
Learning a new script takes practice. [subjectless gerund-participial clause]
The employees working nearby heard the alarm. [post-head subjectless gerund-participial modifier]
The proposal endorsed by the committee was adopted. [post-head subjectless past-participial modifier]

rules.concept: attributive VPs in NPs distinguished from non-finite clauses
rules.statement: Attributive VPs preceding an NP head are not analysed as clauses, even though the same participial verb-form can head a postnominal non-finite clause.
rules.condition: When a gerund-participle or past participle with permitted pre-verbal adverbial modification appears as an attributive modifier before a noun, classify the participial constituent as an attributive VP rather than as a non-finite clause; distinguish it from a postnominal clause functioning as a modifier.

contrast.text: The rapidly approaching ferry sounded its horn. [approaching: attributive VP before noun, not a clause]
The carefully prepared report reached the council. [prepared: attributive VP, not a clause]
The ferry approaching the pier sounded its horn. [post-head gerund-participial clause]
The report prepared by the students reached the council. [post-head past-participial clause]

rules.statement: To-infinitival clauses can have closed- or open-interrogative form and can also function as wh or non-wh relative clauses.
rules.condition: For a to-infinitival clause, recognise whether + to-VP as a closed interrogative, interrogative phrase + to-VP as an open interrogative, relative phrase + to-VP as a wh relative, and an appropriate non-wh relative to-infinitival with for + subject as a relative modifier.

contrast.text: We cannot decide whether to reopen the gallery. [closed interrogative to-infinitival]
Lara asked where to begin. [open interrogative to-infinitival]
The team needs a partner with whom to negotiate. [wh relative to-infinitival]
An assignment for you to complete is ready. [non-wh relative to-infinitival]

rules.concept: non-finite clauses as complements in multiple phrase categories
rules.statement: Non-finite clauses can serve as complements within clause, adjective-phrase, noun-phrase, and preposition-phrase structures, not just as complements of verbs.
rules.condition: When a non-finite subordinate clause is selected or licensed as a complement, determine whether the host is a clause, AdjP, NP or PP; do not label all non-finite dependents as clause-level adjuncts solely because they express purpose or another semantic relation.

contrast.text: Their goal was to cross the valley. [non-finite predicative complement in clause structure]
The explorers were eager to cross the valley. [complement within an AdjP]
They welcomed the chance to cross the valley. [complement within an NP]
The party left early in order to reach the campsite. [non-finite complement in PP structure]

rules.concept: non-finite clauses functioning as modifiers or supplements
rules.statement: Besides complement functions, non-finite clauses may function as clause modifiers, NP modifiers, or prosodically supplementary comments.
rules.condition: When a non-finite clause is not a selected complement, classify a purpose to-infinitival directly modifying a clause as a modifier, a postnominal to-infinitival as an NP modifier, or a detached evaluative/comment to-infinitival as a supplement.

contrast.text: The rescue team left before dawn to avoid the traffic. [modifier in clause structure]
We bought a shelf to store the jars on. [modifier within an NP]
The speech was confusing, to be fair. [supplement to clause]
The festival, to put it mildly, was chaotic. [supplement within a clause]
